newsitem.title: UK: CP Ships takeover of Lykes facing major opposition.
newsitem.headline: CP Ships takeover of Lykes facing major opposition.

text.p: Lykes Bros Steamship Co is trying to put together a deal by the end of this week with US maritime authorities to allow its take-over by Canada's CP Ships to go ahead.

A spokeswoman for the Florida-based container shipping group, which is under Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, said Lykes' chief executive officer Joe Freeman has been in discussions all this week with Washington-based Marad, the Maritime Administration arm of the government.

Freeman is negotiating Marad approval for CP Ships' $30 million takeover of the ailing US group's shipping operations following petitions from rivals Sea-Land Service Inc, a unit of CSX Corp, and International Shipholding Corp opposing the continuation of US subsidies to Lykes if the deal goes ahead.
The Transportation Institute, a maritime association with links to the Seafarers international Union, has also attacked the takeover by CP Ships, a division of Canadian Pacific Ltd .
A Marad spokesman confirmed that talks were going on but said he could give no indication when a decision would be made.
Sea-Land spokesman Clint Eisenhauer said: "Lykes says the clock is ticking and it needs to resolve the issue quickly. Sea-Land is saying time sensitivity should not be over-riding."
"Marad must be sure it has gone through the proper process of due diligence to review all the issues," he added.
The Marad decision has added significance following Singapore's Neptune Orient Lines Ltd proposed $825 million acquisition of US flag-carrier APL Ltd made in April.
Lykes, APL and Sea-Land receive U.S. government subsidies of $2 million a year for every ship which is U.S.-flagged and manned and made available for military use in times of crisis.
The Marad decision on Lykes could set a precedent for the US administration's approach to national carriers being taken over by foreign groups.

Sea-Land's latest petition against the CP Ships takeover, sent on May 12, said the issue is not whether Lykes is allowed to restructure, but whether it can still receive support from a programme designed to encourage US citizens to provide the government with effective and reliable transportation services in time of war or national emergency.

"The Lykes proposal to substitute superficial corporate structures for actual and available US flag intermodal transportation resources cannot be reconciled with the structure or purpose of the Maritime Security Act," it said.

Lykes has claimed that Sea-Land's opposition is an attempt to put a smaller competitor out of business - an allegation that Sea-Land has rejected. - Paul Berrill, Reuters Shipping News + 44 171 542 4087
